title: Larger genera tend to grow larger and dominant forms more dominant

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Larger genera tend to grow larger and dominant forms more dominant

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because the dominant species of larger genera vary most and varieties become new species, larger genera tend to become larger, and dominant forms tend to become more dominant by leaving many modified, dominant descendants.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The larger genera thus tend to become larger; and throughout nature the forms of life which are now dominant tend to become still more dominant by leaving many modified and dominant descendants.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter II, “Variation under Nature”; section “Summary”. Scope: genera and dominant species throughout nature

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch02-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Genus growth is testable with fossil data, but connecting it causally to present dominance and modified dominant descendants requires proxies. Different components are resolvable to different degrees.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Using fossil and dated phylogenetic time slices, test whether initially species-rich genera have higher subsequent net diversification and whether widespread abundant lineages leave more dominant descendants. Positive temporal effects support the prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Dominance has no single cross-taxon measure.

Survivorship bias can create apparent rich-get-richer patterns.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fossil richness trajectories and living ranges can test pieces of a tendency for large and dominant groups to expand. Ancestral dominance and 'modified dominant descendants' are not directly in those tables, so the second half is a proxy. Passive statistical trends and missing extinct side-branches keep a positive pattern from isolating the stated mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Test whether larger genera tend to gain species through time more than smaller ones, and whether species that are widespread and abundant leave more descendant species that are themselves widespread. A positive richness trend and a positive descendant-dominance relationship, above a passive-diffusion null, would support the prediction; large genera shrinking as often as they grow, or dominant species leaving no more dominant descendants, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Abundance and dominance of ancestors are barely preserved, so descendant dominance is proxied by living range.

Large genera are expected to wander more under a passive null, so growth is not automatically a driven trend.

Extant trees lack the failed lineages that would have made dominant groups look less inevitably successful.
